bib.title: The Relationship Between Precision-Recall and ROC Curves
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Pittsburgh, PA

question: How are ROC space and Precision-Recall space related, and what does that imply for curve comparison, interpolation and AUC optimisation on skewed data?
hypothesis: A deep connection exists between ROC and PR space even though PR curves look more informative on highly skewed data.
contributions: For any dataset the ROC curve and PR curve for a given algorithm contain the same points; a curve dominates in ROC space iff it dominates in PR space.
The achievable PR curve, the PR analog of the ROC convex hull, can be computed efficiently via the ROC hull.
Linear interpolation is insufficient between points in PR space; a correct interpolation is given.
An algorithm that optimises AUC-ROC is not guaranteed to optimise AUC-PR.

method.summary: Theoretical analysis with proofs (Theorems 3.1, 3.2, Corollary 3.1), a local-skew interpolation for PR points, and two constructed numeric examples. No models are trained and no real dataset is run in this paper.
method.task: binary classifier evaluation: ROC vs PR curves

datasets.name: Cancer detection dataset (Fig 1)
datasets.source: highly-skewed cancer detection dataset from Davis et al. 2005; size not stated

inference.samples: not applicable; constructed examples, one curve pair each

parameters.local_skew: (FP_B - FP_A)/(TP_B - TP_A); new points at TP_A+x for integer 1<=x<=TP_B-TP_A with FP raised linearly by the local skew
parameters.threshold_construction: sort test-example probabilities; for each i with class(i)!=class(i+1) and prob(i)<prob(i+1), call every example j>=i+1 positive
parameters.tuning_set_protocol: find candidate thresholds and the hull on a tuning set, then apply those thresholds to the test data
parameters.auc_pr: composite trapezoidal method over the interpolated PR points

metrics.name: AUC-ROC
metrics.definition: trapezoidal area under ROC; equivalent to the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney statistic

metrics.name: AUC-PR
metrics.definition: composite trapezoidal area under the interpolated PR curve

baselines: naive curve construction vs convex hull / achievable PR curve (Fig 5)
eval.protocol: Proofs plus worked numeric examples; no seeds or significance tests.

availability.code: Java program for the metrics at http://www.cs.wisc.edu/~richm/programs/AUC/

results.claim: For a fixed dataset a ROC curve and a PR curve are in one-to-one correspondence and contain the same confusion matrices, provided Recall is not 0.
results.setup: Fixed numbers of positives and negatives; Theorem 3.1
results.quote:
Theorem 3.1. For a given dataset of positive and negative examples, there exists a one-to-one correspon-
dence between a curve in ROC space and a curve in PR space, such that the curves contain exactly the same
confusion matrices, if Recall̸ = 0.

results.claim: One curve dominates another in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space.
results.setup: Fixed numbers of positives and negatives; Theorem 3.2
results.quote:
Theorem 3.2. For a ﬁxed number of positive and neg-
ative examples, one curve dominates a second curve in
ROC space if and only if the ﬁrst dominates the second
in Precision-Recall space.

results.claim: Two curves from a constructed 20-positive, 2000-negative domain rank oppositely under AUC-ROC (curve II higher, 0.875 vs 0.813).
results.setup: 20 positives, 2000 negatives, two overlapping convex-hull curves (Fig 7a); value is curve II, curve I is 0.813
results.quote:
The AUC-ROC for curve I is 0.813 and the
AUC-ROC for curve II is 0.875

results.claim: Same two curves under AUC-PR: curve I wins at 0.514 against 0.038 for curve II, the opposite choice.
results.setup: 20 positives, 2000 negatives, same curves as Fig 7; value is curve I, curve II is 0.038
results.quote: The AUC-PR for curve I is now 0.514

results.claim: Linear interpolation in PR space overestimates AUC-PR: interpolation gives 0.031, a straight line gives 0.50.
results.setup: Single point (0.02, 1) extended to endpoints (0, 1) and (1, 0.008); 433 positives, 56,164 negatives (Fig 6); correct interpolation value shown, linear is 0.50
results.quote:
Interpolating as we have described would
have an AUC-PR of 0.031; a linear connection would
severely overestimate with an AUC-PR of 0.50.

results.claim: Correct PR interpolation between A (TP=5, FP=5) and B (TP=10, FP=30) has local skew 5 negatives per positive, and precision falls non-linearly from 0.500 to 0.250.

results.claim: In the cancer detection example ROC curves look near optimal while PR curves show Algorithm 2 clearly better than Algorithm 1.
results.setup: Same learned models on a highly-skewed cancer detection dataset (Davis et al. 2005), Fig 1; no numbers
results.quote:
The performances of the algorithms appear to be com-
parable in ROC space, however, in PR space we can
see that Algorithm 2 has a clear advantage over Algo-
rithm 1.

results.claim: The achievable PR curve is obtained by taking the ROC convex hull, mapping its points to PR space and interpolating correctly; it discards exactly the points under the ROC hull.
results.quote:
Remarkably, when constructing the achievable
PR curve one discards exactly the same points omit-
ted by the convex hull in ROC space.

limits: Constructed examples only; the paper says nothing about how often AUC-ROC and AUC-PR disagree on real data.
Theorem 3.1 fails at Recall = 0 (FP cannot be recovered).
Dominance gives no ranking when curves cross.
The achievable PR curve is not a true convex hull because interpolation is non-linear.
Convex hull must be built on a tuning set, not test data, to keep the train/test split; the test curve then need not be a hull.
Cost curves are mentioned as an alternative and left out of scope.
The Fig 1 dataset size is not stated here; it comes from Davis et al. 2005.
The paper treats AUC-PR by trapezoids over interpolated points; average precision is not discussed.
